Ethernet Fundamentals: What This Module Covers
Ethernet is a family of wired networking technologies used to exchange data between computers, controllers,
sensors, test equipment and other networked devices.
This module explains:
•How Ethernet devices are physically connected
•How devices are identified using MAC (Media Access Control) addresses
•How data is organised into Ethernet frames
•How switches forward frames
•How VLANs (Virtual LANs, or Virtual Local Area Networks) divide a physical network into logical networks
Module Index: Four Parts
Part 1 - Ethernet Basics and the Physical Link: why Ethernet, OSI model, components, naming, media, duplex
and autonegotiation, CSMA/CD
Part 2 - Topologies, Addressing and Switching: topologies, hub/switch/router, MAC addresses, ARP, switch
learning and forwarding, loops and spanning tree
Part 3 - The Ethernet Frame: collision and broadcast domains, frame structure, field walkthrough, EtherType,
padding, frame check sequence
Part 4 - VLANs and Wrap-Up: why VLANs, access and trunk ports, IEEE 802.1Q tag, tagged frame example,
complete flow, summary
Each part opens with its own divider and contents slide, and closes with a knowledge check.

What Is Ethernet?
Definition
Ethernet is a family of networking technologies used primarily for
communication within a local network.
Ethernet standards cover
•How devices connect using a physical medium
•How bits are represented on the medium
•How network interfaces are identified
•How data is organised into frames
•How transmission errors are detected
•How switches forward frames in a local network
IEEE 802.3 defines MAC and PHY variants. IEEE 802.1 covers
bridging, including IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tagging.
Ethernet is not a single item
Ethernet is not only a cable, an RJ45 connector, a data rate, a switch
or an Internet connection. It is a family of physical-layer and data-
link-layer specifications.
Upper-Layer Data
Ethernet Frame
Physical Signal
Cable or Fibre
Received Ethernet Frame
Ethernet converts higher-layer data into a structured frame and transports it across a physical link.

Main Ethernet Components
Communication path
Application Software
OS Network Stack
Ethernet MAC (Media Access Control)
Ethernet PHY (physical layer transceiver)
Connector and Cable
Network
Network Interface Controller
•MAC and PHY
•Transmit and receive buffers
•Processor interface and registers
•Device-driver support
Ethernet MAC
•Creates Ethernet frames
•Adds source and destination MAC addresses
•Identifies the payload protocol
•Transfers frames to and from the PHY
•Processes received frames and error detection
Ethernet PHY
•Converts digital information into physical signals
•Receives signals from the medium and recovers bits
•Performs physical-layer encoding and decoding
•Supports a specified data rate and medium
The MAC handles frames and addresses.
The PHY handles signals and the physical link.
How Two Ethernet Devices Communicate
Point-to-point connection Transmission sequence
•Device A creates an Ethernet frame
•A's MAC passes the frame to its PHY
•The PHY converts the frame into signals
•Signals travel through the medium
•B's PHY recovers the transmitted bits
•B's MAC checks and processes the frame
•The payload goes to the upper-layer protocol
Reverse communication
The same link may simultaneously carry traffic from Device B to
Device A.
MAC-to-MAC communication is carried physically through two
PHYs and the medium between them.
Device A - sender Device B - receiver

Physical Media
Twisted-pair copper
Copper Ethernet cable uses twisted
conductor pairs. Twisting reduces
electromagnetic interference and
crosstalk.
•Economical, widely available, easy to install
•Supports multiple Ethernet data rates
•Commonly supported by network equipment
Considerations: cable category, link length, connector quality, EMI,
routing and pair termination.
Optical fibre
•High bandwidth and longer distance
•Immunity to electromagnetic interference
•Electrical isolation between endpoints
Considerations: optical transceivers, connector handling and
cleanliness, installation cost, mechanical protection.
Different physical media can transport Ethernet frames. The selected PHY must support the required medium and data rate.
Choose copper when: Shorter distance | lower cost | simple
installation, standard equipment
Choose fibre when: Longer distance | high EMI environment |
electrical isolation required
Optical fibre carries the data as light
through a glass core, so no electrical
signal travels on the link.
Simplex, Half Duplex and Full Duplex
Simplex
Device A Device B
Communication occurs in only one direction.
Half duplex
Both devices can transmit, but not simultaneously.
Full duplex
Both devices can transmit and receive at the same time.
Ethernet context
•Shared legacy Ethernet used half-duplex communication
•Modern switch-to-device links commonly run full duplex
•Full-duplex point-to-point links have no shared collision condition
Example
At time t1:
A transmits a frame to B
At the same time:
B transmits a frame to A
Result:
Both proceed on a full-duplex link
Full-duplex Ethernet supports simultaneous transmission and
reception over a point-to-point link.
Device A Device B
Device A Device B
Autonegotiation: How a Link Agrees Speed and Duplex
Step 1: Both PHYs advertise
Each PHY advertises its supported speeds and duplex modes
Exchanged as link pulses before any frame is sent
Step 2: The highest common mode wins
Both ends select the best capability they share
e.g. 1000 Mb/s full duplex when both support it
Step 3: The link comes up
Link established at the agreed speed and duplex
The port reports link up and data can flow
Legacy 10/100BASE-T mismatch
One end forced, the other autonegotiating
Parallel detection finds speed, but not duplex.
The negotiating end uses half duplex. A mismatch occurs if the forced end uses full
duplex. Other PHYs may behave differently or fail to link.
Rule of thumb
Prefer autonegotiation at both ends
Use forced settings only when the PHY supports them
Autonegotiation selects a common operating mode. Link-startup
and configuration rules depend on the PHY.
A legacy duplex mismatch can leave the link up but cause late collisions, CRC
errors and poor throughput. Do not apply this fallback rule to every Ethernet
PHY.
Shared Ethernet and CSMA/CD
Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection
In a shared network, several devices used the same medium. If two
transmitted at nearly the same time, their signals could interfere and
cause a collision.
Clarification
CSMA/CD applies to shared half-duplex Ethernet. It is not the normal
mechanism of a modern full-duplex switched link. IEEE 802.3 covers
both modes.
Key terms
Jam signal: a short burst sent after a collision so every device on the segment
knows the transmission failed.
Backoff: each device waits a random time before retrying, so they do not collide
again immediately.
Collisions belong to shared half-duplex Ethernet.
Switched full-duplex links remove the shared collision condition.

Listen to the shared medium
Is the medium
idle?

•A. Ethernet MAC

•C. Connector

Question 3
Where is CSMA/CD relevant?
•A. Shared half-duplex Ethernet
•B. Full-duplex switched Ethernet
•C. IP routing
